blockMcqs.question: Which standard defines WiFi wireless networking?
options: IEEE 802.3
IEEE 802.11
IEEE 802.15
IEEE 802.1Q
blockMcqs.explanation: IEEE 802.11 is the standard family for WiFi. 802.3 is Ethernet; 802.15 is Bluetooth; 802.1Q is VLAN tagging.

blockMcqs.question: What is the hidden node problem in wireless?
options: A node hides its SSID from other devices
Two nodes out of range collide at a shared receiver
A node drops packets when signal is strong
An AP refuses connections to far devices
blockMcqs.explanation: Two senders that can't hear each other both sense a free channel and transmit simultaneously, causing a collision at the receiver they share.

blockMcqs.question: What does SSID stand for?
options: Shared Signal ID
Subnet Scope Identifier
Service Set Identifier
Spectrum Source Index
blockMcqs.explanation: SSID (Service Set Identifier) is the human-readable network name broadcast by an access point.

blockMcqs.question: In CSMA/CA, what is the purpose of the random backoff?
options: Increase transmission power
Spread retries so multiple waiters don't collide again
Compress the data before sending
Request a dedicated channel from the AP
blockMcqs.explanation: Random backoff reduces the chance that all waiting nodes retry at exactly the same moment, which would cause another collision.

blockMcqs.question: Why does 5 GHz WiFi have less congestion than 2.4 GHz?
options: It uses stronger encryption
It has more non-overlapping channels
Fewer devices support it at all
It operates at lower power
blockMcqs.explanation: 5 GHz provides ~25 non-overlapping channels vs 3 at 2.4 GHz, so neighboring networks are far less likely to interfere.

blockMcqs.question: What happens during a cellular handoff?
options: The device switches WiFi bands automatically
The active connection transfers from one cell tower to another
The SIM card is re-authenticated with the network
5G downgrades to 4G during poor coverage
blockMcqs.explanation: Handoff (handover) is the seamless transfer of an active connection between base stations as the device moves between cells.

blockMcqs.question: Why is WEP considered broken?
options: It requires a physical key to connect
Its encryption can be cracked in minutes
It only works on 5 GHz networks
It blocks mobile devices by default
blockMcqs.explanation: WEP's RC4 implementation has known cryptographic flaws. Attackers can recover the key in minutes by capturing enough packets.

blockMcqs.question: What is multipath fading in wireless networks?
options: Signal strength loss from using multiple antennas
Interference when reflected signal copies arrive at different times
A routing loop across multiple access points
Packet loss during cellular handoff
blockMcqs.explanation: Reflected copies of the same signal travel different distances and arrive out of phase, causing constructive or destructive interference at the receiver.
